subject: Computing log probability via an externally linked C++ library (Help!)

messages.author: 1090ec6e2018fcc1
messages.subject: Computing log probability via an externally linked C++ library (Help!)
parts:
I'm new to cmdstan-2.8, but have already applied it successfully in a few domains in geophysics. In an application I'm currently working on, I have a C++ library that computes a log posterior probability for seismic scatterer locations, given some seismic waveforms. Since it would be extremely burdensome to recode the C++ library in stan, my approach was to write some stan code whose resulting hpp file could be revised to include my C++ library. To do this I wrote the following stan code (see below). The first function, modelSetup, is a placeholder that I rewrite in the stan hpp file to load the seismic waveforms along with some supplementary information and puts them in a global variable that I can access from my second function. The second function, setLogProb, is a placeholder that I rewrite in the stan hpp file to call my external C++ library for a log probability value. I put printouts in my C++ code to verify that stan is properly passing the scatterer x and z locations (also seismic velocity vel). All seems well so far.

BUT, when I compile and run the stan-generated (and me modified) hpp code, the uncertainty in the (x,z) locations is much smaller that I know is true (because I have plotted the PDF for simple cases over the entire domain.

QUESTION:
I'm wondering if there is something is stan that produces incorrect sampling when external libraries are used. Also, I wonder if there is an easier way to link to external libraries that through editing the stan-generated hpp file.

Michael

// Stan code
functions {
  void modelSetup() {
  }

  real setLogProb(vector x, vector z, real vel) {
    return 0.;
  }
}
data {
  int numScat;
  real velocityMean;
  real velocitySDev;
}
transformed data {
  modelSetup();
}
parameters {
  vector[numScat] x;
  vector[numScat] z;
  real vel;
}
transformed parameters {
}
model {
  // Priors
  vel ~ normal(velocityMean, velocitySDev);

  // Likelihood
  increment_log_prob(setLogProb(x, z, vel));
}

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: Computing log probability via an externally linked C++ library (Help!)
parts:
Hi Michael,

Stan's math library does two things: lets you calculate the log densities and also their derivatives.  I imagine what's happening is that your external code is happily providing the log probability values but not correctly updating the derivatives so you get inaccurate results.  If you can provide those derivatives you could interface your function correctly but it may be easier to re-code the library's function via the Stan math library and just get the derivatives for 'free'.

Krzysztof

Krzysztof,

Thank your the rapid reply.

I suspected as much. If I were to compute the Jacobian in my C++ library, what Stan function would I used to update its value in Stan?

If I choose to reimplement my code in Stan, is there a way to gain access to the Eigen FFT function? I don't see an FFT in the Stan documentation, but there is reference to Stan's use of it in computing the effective sample size.

Michael

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Computing log probability via an externally linked C++ library (Help!)
parts:
We haven't exposed FFT functions, so you'd have to
define derivatives there or rely on the dicey proposition
of differentiating the FFT code (which you might be able to
do if it's templated generally enough in Eigen).

To add functions to Stan itself, there are two routes.
You can either write them in Stan directly, in which case autodiff
will compute the derivatives, or you can actually build a new
function into the Stan language and compile it in. The latter's
more efficient if you have analytic derivatives and can also
be more stable if the computation is "approximate" --- you want
to approximate the derivative, not take derivatives of the
approximation. The latter can work in some cases -- you can always
test with finite diffs to see if you have enough tolerance (we're
actually not sure when tolerance in functions would cause problems).

Adding functions to Stan is more involved. See:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

- Bob
